p.d: Directions : Read the passage given below and answer the questions that follow by selecting the most appropriate option.
p.b: Law is found in all modern societies and is usually regarded as the bedrock of civilized existence. But what distinguishes law from other social rules, and in what sense does law operate at an international or even global level? Is there such a thing as international law? In the case of domestic law, it is relatively easy to identify a series of distinguishing characteristics. First, law is made by the government and so applies throughout society. Not only does this mean that law reflects the will of the state and therefore takes precedence over all other norms and social rules, but it also gives domestic law universal jurisdiction within a particular political society. Second, law is compulsory; citizens are not allowed to choose which laws to obey and which to ignore, because law is backed up by a system of coercion and punishment. Law thus requires the existence of a legal system, a set of norms and institutions through which legal rules are created, interpreted and enforced. Third, law has a 'public' quality in that it consists of codified, published and recognised rules. This is, in part, achieved by enacting law through a formal and usually public, legislative process. Moreover, punishments handed down for law breaking are predictable and can be anticipated."

p.d: Directions : Read the passage given below and answer the questions that follow by selecting the most appropriate option.
p.b: To avoid the various foolish opinions to which mankind is prone, no superhuman brain is required. A few simple rules keep you free, not from all errors, but from silly errors. If the matter is one that can be settled by observation, make the observation yourself. Aristotle could have avoided the mistake of thinking that women have fewer teeth than men, by the simple device of asking Mrs. Aristotle to keep her mouth open while he counted. He did not do so because he thought he knew. Thinking that you know, when in fact you do not, is a fatal mistake to which we are all prone. I believe myself that hedgehogs eat black beetles, because I have been told that they do; but if I was writing a book on the habits of hedgehogs, I should not commit myself until I had seen one enjoying this diet. Aristotle, however, was less cautious. Ancient and medieval writers knew all about unicorns and salamanders; not one of them thought it necessary to avoid dogmatic statements about them because he had never seen one of them.

p.d: Directions : Read the passage given below and answer the questions that follow by selecting the most appropriate option.
p.b: On the morning of August 31, 1573, 3000 horsemen of the imperial Mughal army paused at the bank of the Sabarmati. The rebels, they were after, lay just beyond the swollen river but the soldiers were exhausted: they had travelled 960 kilometers of difficult terrain in nine days, riding almost continuously. Suddenly a warrior on a chestnut charger plunged into the raging torrent. As man and horse struggled on to the opposite bank, a thrill ran through the army. It was the emperor, Jalaluddin Akbar! With a roar, the soldiers followed him across and within two days, they had put down the rebellion so thoroughly that Gujarat remained in Mughal hands for the next 185 years.

p.d: Directions : Read the passage given below and answer the questions that follow by selecting the most appropriate option.
p.b: There exists a language older than words, spoken not through the tongue but through textures, colours, rhythms and silences. It is the language of nature — a soft, persistent whisper that surrounds us, though few have the patience to listen. In the rustling of leaves, the migration of birds, the bloom of a lone flower amidst a barren field, nature offers a narrative both timeless and ever-changing. At dawn, the sky does not shout but blushes in subtle hues of amber and rose, as though shy to announce the new day. Trees sway not with urgency but with quiet grace, teaching that strength and stillness are not opposing forces. The river, unhurried, carries through mountains and meadows alike, murmuring ancient truths about perseverance and purpose. Even the decay of autumn, so often associated with death, carries within it the promise of renewal, of a spring yet to come. Yet, in our rush to modernize, we have dulled our senses to these subtle signs. We measure success in speed and numbers, often forgetting that not all value can be calculated. Technology may have extended our reach, but it has also narrowed our gaze. ---

p.d: Directions : Read the passage given below and answer the questions that follow by selecting the most appropriate option.
p.b: Technological advancement has undeniably transformed human life, often for the better. Innovations in medicine, communications and transportation have expanded horizons and improved living standards. Yet, there remains an underlying paradox: as societies become more technologically advanced, individuals often report feeling more disconnected, anxious and overwhelmed. This contradiction is not merely anecdotal. Numerous studies suggest a correlation between digital dependency and declining mental well-being. The convenience of instant communication, for instance, has paradoxically eroded the depth of interpersonal relationships. Similarly, the promise of efficiency brought by automation and artificial intelligence has, in some sectors, resulted in job displacement and a growing sense of purposelessness. Moreover, the constant pursuit of progress has fostered a culture of perpetual urgency. The pressure to stay updated, to be productive and to remain relevant has blurred the boundaries between personal and professional lives. Instead of liberating individuals, modern technologies often act as invisible shackles, tethering them to devices and schedules. ---

p.d: Directions : Read the passage given below and answer the questions that follow by selecting the most appropriate option.
p.b: The celebration of "workaholism" has long been a foundational pillar of corporate culture. Employees who routinely sacrifice their sleep, personal relationships and leisure time are consistently rewarded with promotions and public praise. This glorification of constant busyness treats human labour as a machine that can run indefinitely without maintenance. However, this hyper-productive ethos masks a deeper structural crisis: severe mental burnout and a collapse of employee well-being. When a workspace transforms into a pressure cooker of endless deadlines, creativity is ironically the very first casualty. True innovation requires cognitive breathing room — periods of stillness where the brain can connect unrelated ideas. By chaining individuals to a relentless cycle of immediate reactive tasks, organizations trade long-term creative breakthroughs for short-term, superficial productivity metrics. This toxic environment does not just harm the individual worker. It eventually erodes the collective intellectual capital of the enterprise itself, proving that the cult of endless hustle is ultimately a self-defeating strategy. ---

p.d: Directions : Read the passage given below and answer the questions that follow by selecting the most appropriate option.
p.b: Patience is better than wisdom An ounce of patience is worth a pound of brains. All men praise patience, but few can practise it. It is medicine which is good for all diseases, but it is not every garden that grows the herbs to make it with. Many people are born crying, live complaining and die disappointed. They think every other person's burden to be light and their own feathers to be heavy as lead, and yet if the truth were known, it is their fancy rather than their fate that makes things go so hard with them. Many would be well off if they could but think so. ---
